title: Bass and percussion; strong beat on two and four
summary: He explains the bass as melodic and rhythmic and Cuban rhythm's strong beats.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: The bass play two different commitment i the orchestra. A base is a melodic instrument, a rhythm instrument. That's in all the instruments that I know. The bass and the piano. They got two (unintelligible). Melodic and rhythm. That's the ________ instrument, the bass.
So the bass player lays down a pattern, right? A pattern on which the percussion build?

Yes. Because if you can play cha-cha-cha, cha-cha-cha got this (unintelligible) rhythm. It's a bass foundation for that particular rhythm. You play ________, it's another, the distinct and different ________ rhythm.
In every Cuban rhythm that I know, the first foundation is between -- the first foundation is the skin instruments. Then --
How do they relate to each other?

Well, somebody is smarter than me, more prepared than me, create ________, a bass that will go right along with a skin instrument, so don't interfere, to create more power in the rhythm, and that's why they work in an opposite way. If you listen to Cuban music, you will know that the rhythm instrument and the bass is two potential crossfire rhythms. That's what Dizzy Gillespie said to me one day. He said, you listen to that, and you understand how the common people -- where's the downbeat for the common people. I said,
I don't know, but our music has developed that way.
You got to feel the downbeat, because you never going to look for an instrument to give a downbeat because we don't play that way. This music is basic in the two and the fourth beat.

And the other Latin American countries, the average Latin American country, their rhythm, their foundation is one and three. Always downbeat on the -- Cuban is (unintelligible). What the American jazz drummer player would do in the last of the snare drum. Now, I put it to you more simple.

That's what I've been telling people all my life, nobody want to listen to, but that's the difference between Cuban music and the other Latin American countries is our rhythm -- the foundation of our rhythm is completely different. The strong beat in the Cuban music is in the second and the fourth. And you take the tango, it's downbeat. You take the Columbian music, downbeat. You take a marengo, the strong beat is the downbeat. You never hear -- the other day I went to the company and they wanted me to record. And they said my music was terrific. The disco music is what they want.
